Find the $y$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y={x}^{2}-\sqrt{2}x$ that is closest to the point $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$ Do not round the answer.

$y=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={(x-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-\sqrt{2}x+\frac{1}{2}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-\sqrt{2}x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+\frac{1}{2}+{y}^{2} \\  & ={y}^{2}+y+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y+1 & =0 \\ 2y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=-\frac{1}{2}.$
